message.content:
{
  "frontend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement the frontend changes to work with backend soft-delete behavior. Follow these concrete instructions and verify with the acceptance tests below. Do not change authorization semantics; if any behavior is ambiguous, ask backend owners before implementing.

Scope (apply to every resource that currently supports DELETE, GET (collection and single), PUT, and count):
- UI-level behavior must treat deleted items as non-existent where specified below (lists, counts, GET/PUT).

Required changes:
1) API contract handling
  - The backend will add a nullable field deleted_at to resource representations. Treat deleted_at as an optional ISO 8601 / RFC 3339 UTC timestamp (e.g., 2021-08-19T12:34:56Z) or null. Update any JSON decoding/typing to accept deleted_at?: string | null.
  - Do not assume deleted_at will always be present for old backend versions; keep parsing tolerant.

2) Lists and counts
  - For collection/list views and for any count displayed to users, exclude items with deleted_at != null. That means:
    - When rendering a list fetched from the collection endpoint, do not show items that have deleted_at set.
    - When showing any total counts supplied by the backend, use the count value returned by the backend (backend will exclude deleted entries). Do not perform client-side filtering that would contradict backend count; instead rely on backend count for authoritative totals.

3) Detail GET and PUT
  - If a GET for a single item returns 404, show the standard “not found” UX.
  - If a PUT returns 404 because the item is deleted, show the same “not found” UX.
  - Do not convert a 404 from a deleted resource into a permission error UI.

4) DELETE behavior in the UI
  - When user triggers DELETE on an item, call the DELETE API as before.
  - If the DELETE is successful (first deletion), continue to display the same success message and UX already used in the product for that successful deletion (preserve the original success message and status handling exactly).
  - If the DELETE returns 404 (this indicates the item was already soft-deleted), show the standard “not found” UX rather than a success message. If the delete request returns 403, show the same permission-denied UX currently used for forbidden operations.
  - Do not treat 404 from a repeated delete as a permission failure.

5) Display of deleted_at
  - If resource details or public listings display metadata, add support to render deleted_at when present. Treat deleted_at as nullable: if null/absent, show nothing. If non-null, display it formatted as UTC RFC 3339 (or use a friendly localized display but keep the underlying value as the RFC3339 string in logs/debug views).

6) Error/permission semantics and ordering
  - Preserve existing permission error UX: operations that lack permission must continue to display the same forbidden behavior (403). Do not mask permission errors by converting them to 404s.
  - Clarify with backend whether authorization checks run before or after the deleted-at existence check for requests that target deleted items. If current system returns 403 for unauthorized requests on existing resources, preserve that ordering. If this is unclear, stop and request confirmation from backend owners. (Do not guess ordering in code.)

7) Tests and QA
  - Add frontend unit/integration tests for these scenarios for each resource UI:
    a) List excludes entries returned by backend with deleted_at != null.
    b) Count shown equals backend-provided count (backend excludes deleted entries).
    c) GET of deleted item -> show not-found.
    d) PUT of deleted item -> show not-found.
    e) First DELETE call (backend success) -> show existing success message.
    f) Repeated DELETE call by authorized user that returns 404 -> show not-found (do not show success).
    g) DELETE attempt without permission that returns 403 -> show permission denied UX.
  - Add e2e/integration tests simulating backend responses for deleted_at values and 403/404/200 sequencing.

Deployment notes / compatibility
  - Backend must be deployed before or at the same time as frontend so that deleted_at appears and list/count semantics are consistent. Ensure frontend tolerates responses without deleted_at (backwards-compatible parsing) to avoid runtime errors during a staggered rollout.

Questions to confirm before implementing (do not guess):
  - Confirm exact API endpoints and resource names to update (use the official API spec). The prompt uses generic resource endpoints; map these instructions to the actual endpoints in the app.
  - Confirm whether authorization checks should be performed before or after the deleted status check for requests targeting deleted items. Preserve whatever current behavior is; if unspecified, ask backend owners.

Acceptance criteria (to verify in QA):
  - Existing DELETE permission model unchanged: unauthorized DELETE attempts still show 403.
  - First successful DELETE returns the same success message as before.
  - Repeated DELETE by an authorized user results in 404 and frontend shows not-found UX.
  - Lists and counts shown in UI exclude deleted items and match backend-provided counts.
  - GET and PUT requests for deleted entries produce not-found UX (404)."
  },
  "backend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement backend changes to convert hard deletes into soft deletes and to ensure API semantics and data migration meet the specified acceptance criteria. Follow these concrete implementation steps and test cases. Do not invent missing contract decisions; if anything below is ambiguous for your codebase (DB type, exact endpoints, existing response payloads/status codes), stop and request clarification.

Scope (apply to every resource that currently supports DELETE, GET (collection and single), PUT, and count):
- Implement soft-delete using a nullable timestamp column deleted_at as described below. Update all read and write handlers and the API representation.

Database / Schema
1) Add column
  - Add a nullable timestamp column named deleted_at to each resource table (exact column naming must match existing conventions; if your DB uses snake_case, use deleted_at). The column must represent a timezone-aware timestamp and be stored/normalized as UTC.
  - If your database type requires a specific type (e.g., TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE in Postgres), use the canonical timezone-aware type for that DB.

2) Data migration for existing rows
  - Create a migration that adds deleted_at with default NULL. Set deleted_at = NULL for all existing rows explicitly as part of the migration (to make intent explicit). Existing rows must not be treated as deleted.

API behavior changes
3) DELETE handler
  - Change the DELETE endpoint so that it performs a soft delete: set deleted_at = current UTC timestamp (serialized/stored as UTC) for the target row instead of removing it from the DB.
  - Preserve the exact response body and status code the API currently returns to clients on the first successful delete. Do not change the success message or status code returned the first time a resource is deleted.
  - If the resource targeted by the DELETE is already soft-deleted (deleted_at != null), return 404 Not Found. (Important: do not return success or 410; return 404.)
  - Keep the existing permission check semantics: if a request is not authorized to delete the resource, return 403 as before. Do not change permission checks into 404s. If ordering of authorization vs deleted check is ambiguous in your codebase, confirm policy with product/ownership: preserve current ordering; do not guess.

4) GET (single resource) and PUT
  - If a GET for a single resource finds the row but deleted_at != null, return 404 Not Found.
  - If a PUT finds the row but deleted_at != null, return 404 Not Found.
  - These 404 responses are used to indicate the resource does not exist (it was deleted).

5) Collection listing and count
  - Collection endpoints must exclude soft-deleted rows: add WHERE deleted_at IS NULL to list queries.
  - Any backend-provided counts (total counts for pagination, API count fields) must exclude soft-deleted rows and match the filtered list. Ensure pagination metadata (total pages, total count) is computed using the filtered set.

6) API representation / serialization
  - Add deleted_at as a nullable field in the public API representation for the resource. When deleted_at is null, serialize as null or omit the field per existing style (prefer explicit null if your API typically includes the key). When non-null, serialize as RFC 3339 / ISO 8601 UTC (e.g., 2021-08-19T12:34:56Z).
  - Ensure JSON schemas/openapi definitions are updated to mark deleted_at as nullable datetime, so clients can update types accordingly.

7) Authorization semantics and ordering
  - Preserve existing authorization semantics. Do not convert 403 responses to 404 for permission failures. If current codebase performs authorization checks before existence checks (or vice versa), preserve that order unless product owners instruct otherwise. If ordering is not clear, request confirmation from product/security owners. (Do not make a unilateral change.)

8) Migrations and backward compatibility
  - Deploy DB migration that adds deleted_at (nullable) before or together with the code that references the column. Ensure that the API continues to function for older clients during rollout: serializing deleted_at is additive and should be backward-compatible.
  - Ensure indexes used for typical queries are updated/added if necessary (e.g., add an index on deleted_at or on (deleted_at, id) to keep list queries performant) depending on data volume. Confirm with DB/ops team; do not assume index naming or requirements.

Testing and QA
9) Automated tests
  - Unit tests for repository/ORM layer:
    a) Soft delete sets deleted_at to a UTC timestamp (assert timezone awareness or string format per DB driver).
    b) Repeated soft delete attempts return resource-not-found (404) once deleted.
    c) Existing rows are null after migration.
  - Integration/API tests:
    a) DELETE on an existing authorized resource: returns the same success status and body as before.
    b) DELETE on an already-deleted resource by an authorized user: returns 404.
    c) DELETE attempt by an unauthorized user on an existing resource: returns 403.
    d) GET/PUT on a deleted resource: return 404.
    e) List endpoints: returned list excludes deleted entries and pagination/count matches filtered set.
  - Add tests that assert deleted_at is serialized as RFC3339 UTC.

10) Migration rollout and coordination
  - Coordinate deployment so that the DB migration and backend code are deployed in a safe order (add column first if code expects it). The API change adding a nullable field is additive and should be backward-compatible. Ensure CI/feature flags or phased rollout if your deployment strategy requires it.

11) Logging and observability
  - Log soft-deletes (audit log) with actor id, resource id, timestamp (UTC), and previous deleted_at state if relevant.
  - Ensure monitoring/alerts for unexpected high rates of soft-deletes.

Acceptance criteria (automatable):
  - Migration exists and sets deleted_at = NULL for existing rows.
  - DB has a nullable timezone-aware deleted_at column for all affected resources.
  - DELETE sets deleted_at to current UTC timestamp and returns the original success response for the first deletion.
  - Repeated DELETE returns 404 for already soft-deleted resources.
  - GET and PUT on deleted resources return 404.
  - List endpoints and backend counts exclude deleted entries and pagination metadata is consistent with filtered results.
  - API serialization includes deleted_at as nullable RFC3339 UTC value.
  - Authorization errors remain 403 as before; do not convert permission failures into 404s.

Questions to confirm before implementation (do not guess):
  - Confirm exact resource/table names and the DB type (Postgres, MySQL, etc.) so migrations and timestamp column types can be generated accordingly.
  - Confirm the current DELETE success response (status code and body) so it can be preserved exactly for the first delete.
  - Confirm ordering policy: should authorization checks be applied before or after checking deleted status for a request that targets a deleted item? Preserve current behavior; if unclear, request confirmation.

If any of the above items are not directly mappable to your codebase (naming, DB types, or middleware ordering), stop and request the mapping from the product/architecture owners instead of guessing."
  }
}
